en: The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Most Victorious Lamp-King of the East, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of North India during the Great Sui Dynasty.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī, among the solitary...
In a vihāra,
together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus and a multitude of forty thousand great bodhisattvas.
The Brahmā King, Lord of the Sahā World; Śakra Devendra;
and the Four Great Kings: Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, and Vaiśravaṇa.
The Heavenly King Virūpākṣa and the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa,
leading the great generals of the twenty-eight classes of spirits and ghosts,
as well as eighty-four thousand such devas.
Kālika brought his son and all his retinue to sit together in the assembly.
At that time, passing from this Buddha-world through a hundred thousand billion buddha-fields, there was a world named Saṃkusumita.
The Buddha is named Most Victorious Lamp King Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha;
he currently dwells there, preaching the Dharma,
and has dispatched two bodhisattvas.
One was named Great Light and the second was named Immeasurable Light;
they addressed him, saying:
"O son of good family, you should uphold these dharani phrases."
Upon arriving in the Sahā world to join Śākyamuni Buddha,
this dhāraṇī will bring great benefit and be able to ensure that sentient beings dwell in peace and security throughout the long night.
One shall obtain great and wholesome benefits, as well as physical vigor and renown.
Then he spoke the mantra:

*Hre / Mahāhre / Hreṇi / Akkhi makki yōṅ (in Wu dialect) samandi / Mahāsamandi / Sayi saraṃsi / Svāhā.* At that time, the two Bodhisattvas received and upheld these words of the dhāraṇī from the Buddha.
Just as a strong man might bend or extend his arm,
he vanished from the Land of Many Flowers and arrived at the Ghoṣitārāma in the Jeta Grove of Śrāvastī.
Then the two bodhisattvas prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One,
beyond a hundred thousand billion buddha-fields from this buddha-world,”
There is a world named Saṃkusumita.
Therein dwells the Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Varapradīparāja,
who currently resides and teaches the Dharma.
We have been sent to inquire after the World-Honored One’s health and freedom from affliction,
and whether the assembly of disciples is not being troubled by either Māras, ghosts, devas, nāgas, or yakṣas.
Whether they be pūtanas, or piśācas, or pretas, or manustas, or gandharvas, or those who cause madness,
or those who cause the mind to become deranged.
Whether it be demons that obstruct the path, or the ghosts of risen corpses,
or the demons that cause illness on the first, second, third, or fourth day,
or the sun, moon, and lunar mansions, or lions, tigers, and leopards.
It is impossible for venomous snakes, wolves, dogs, bats, humans,
or non-humans to come and cause harm to one who is thus fearful; such a thing cannot occur.
Ānanda, if there are sons or daughters of good family who receive,
uphold, read, recite, copy, explain,
and cause this dharani-phrase to be widely disseminated.
Fire cannot burn them; they do not die by drowning.
Blades cannot wound them, and poisons cannot harm them.
Even kings do not execute them, and the Brahmā gods and others do not harbor resentment toward them.
One can personally recollect the events of ten lifetimes.
Ānanda, this mantra was spoken by seventy-seven billion Buddhas.
Should anyone violate this mantra or those who uphold it, their vital essence will be snatched away.
This would constitute an infringement, a violation, and a transgression against all these Buddhas.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat and adjusted his robes.
Baring his right shoulder and placing his right knee upon the ground,
he joined his palms in *añjali* and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One,
I now also wish to proclaim dhāraṇī phrases for the benefit of sentient beings."
May they obtain excellent benefits, physical strength, and renown.
Then he spoke this mantra:

Aṅge vaṅge | aṅge kuaṅge | anuvarte | varadavati | dūrumai | lūrumai | anāgasi | prāṇāgasi | kasi | mahākasi | anuta | parānuta | khaci | mahākhaci | sthātṛtīre | dantitīre | mire | citi | śiri | bhūme | mahābhūme | bhūbhūme | bhūśapate | svāhā. At that time, the Buddha again addressed Ānanda.
You should receive, uphold, recite, transcribe,
and explain this dhāraṇī phrase, causing it to spread widely. Why is that?
Ānanda, this mantra enables one to personally recollect the events of thirteen lifetimes.
Ānanda, this mantra was spoken by eighty-four billion Buddhas.
Should anyone violate this mantra or those who uphold it, their vital essence shall be seized.
This would constitute an act of infringement, destruction, and opposition toward all these Buddhas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince,
rose from his seat and adjusted his robes.
Baring his right shoulder and placing his right knee upon the ground,
he joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I now also wish to proclaim dhāraṇī phrases in order to bring benefit to sentient beings."
May they obtain wholesome benefits, physical strength, and renown.
Then he spoke this mantra:
A-khya-ke | Sa-kye | Na-ghi | Na-ghi-ni | Na-ghi-sa-le | Bha-na-ni-li | Vau-ha-yi | Vau-ha-ra-pa-ti | Dhyā-na-ti-yi | Dhyā-na-ti-ra-pa-ti | Svāhā. At that time, the Buddha again addressed Ānanda.
You should receive, uphold, recite, copy, explain,
and cause this dharani phrase to be widely disseminated. Why is that?
Ānanda, this mantra enables one to personally recollect the events of thirteen lifetimes.
Ānanda, this mantra was spoken together by ninety-nine billion Buddhas of the past.
If anyone violates this mantra or those who uphold it, their vital essence shall be seized;
this would constitute an offense against and a violation of all these Buddhas.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed the great assembly.
I now also wish to proclaim the phrases of this dhāraṇī to benefit sentient beings,
so that they may obtain wholesome benefits, physical strength,
and renown. He then spoke the mantra:
Āhan, vāhan, yāhan, kūyāhan, dandi, godandi, rāḍre, lūlūre, khire, bhīre, yāhre, svāhā. At that time, the Buddha again addressed Ānanda.
You should receive, uphold, recite, transcribe, explain,
and widely disseminate these dhāraṇī phrases. Why is this?
Ānanda, this mantra was spoken by all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
It universally eliminates all calamities, demonic affairs, and fetters,
and protects [the name of] such-and-such a person, causing them to attain peace and security.
Whether there be diseases caused by poison, or diseases of wind and cold,
or diseases that eliminate the bodily constituents, or pain in the heart, abdomen, and spine;
or pain in the eyes, ears, and body, as well as headaches.
Regarding such afflictions as these,
the Tathāgata Supreme Lamp King has sent these dhāraṇī phrases to bestow upon the World-Honored One.
Furthermore, I desire to cause the sentient beings of this Sahā world to dwell in peace and security throughout the long night,
and to obtain great and virtuous benefits, physical strength, and renown.
He then recited the dhāraṇī as above.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, ensured their lives would not end prematurely.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If you enter among bandits, you should recite this mantra."
If one enters fire or water, or wishes to go to the royal palace,
one should likewise recite this mantra.
If there are various instances of conflict, strife, illness, or fear, one should do the same.
One should likewise keep this mantra in mind.
Whether there be kings, thieves, water, or fire;
or whether there be devas, nāgas, or yakṣas—
Whether they be pūtanas, or puṭṭanās, or piśācas;
whether they be pretas, or gandharvas,
or those who cause madness, or those who cause the mind to become deranged.
Whether it be spirits that obstruct the path, spirits that raise up corpses, spirits that suck away the vital essence of humans,
spirits that cause illness on the first, second, third, or fourth day,
or spirits of the sun, moon, and constellations, or lions, tigers, and leopards.
Whether it be venomous snakes, wolves, dogs, or bats,
or whether they be humans or non-humans who come to harass and harm them,
there is no possibility that those who feel fear will exist.
Ānanda, if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, sons of good family,
or daughters of good family who receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, explain,
and cause this dhāraṇī phrase to be widely disseminated;
Fire cannot burn them; they do not die by drowning.
Blades cannot wound them; poisons cannot harm them; they do not perish on the road.
If one ties a thread consecrated with this mantra upon a withered tree, [the same protection shall prevail].
If even these can be moved by seeking compassion and protection to return to life as flowers and fruit,
how much more so for human beings?
This is true except in the case of karmic retribution from past deeds whose results are already fixed.
Ānanda, if one recites and practices at the three times— early morning, midday, and evening—
without allowing for any neglect or abandonment,
grave offenses will become light.
If one facing the death penalty receives a flogging, it shall immediately cease.
One who should have been flogged shall instead receive a reprimand and thus immediately cease.
If there is something sought, one will immediately obtain a superior resolve.
By the power of this divine mantra,
and because they are protected and mindful of by all Buddhas and holy beings,
at that time the Four Great Heavenly Kings...
He immediately rose from his seat,
adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground,
joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One."

I now likewise wish to proclaim the phrases of this dhāraṇī to benefit sentient beings, so that they may obtain wholesome benefits, physical strength, and renown. Should there be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—
One should uphold, recite, copy, and explain this dharani-phrase, causing it to be widely disseminated.
Should there be any evil persons or non-humans, [who might cause harm...]
Unable to find an opportunity, he then spoke this mantra:
*Tadyathā | dandadanda chape | vidanchape | tathāyapani | dhanhuchape | ghoṣakani | ghughurani ghughurani | damale | chamale svāhā*. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
This dhāraṇī sūtra was previously taught by all Buddhas;
I now likewise expound it clearly to benefit all sentient beings.
If anyone possesses a heart of faith and joy, they shall hear and uphold this mantra.
One’s eloquence will increase, and wherever one goes or comes,
one shall not encounter any calamities; neither humans nor non-humans,
nor kumbhāṇḍas nor pūtanas, shall be able to cause harm or affliction.
By reciting and upholding this mantra, one shall not be killed by others;
by reciting and upholding this mantra, even Māra Pāpīyān,
the Lord of Heaven who is preeminent within the desire realm, shall be unable to create obstacles.
By reciting and upholding this sutra, parents, brothers, kinsmen,
and close friends shall not encounter any misfortunes or calamities;
by reciting and upholding this sutra, for hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas—
Even the commission of unwholesome karma— the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes—
can be extinguished within seven days by reciting and upholding this mantra. Thus,
the Bodhisattva has accumulated all manner of meritorious virtues throughout billions of kalpas.
By reciting and upholding this mantra for seven days, one can bring about excellence.
The four great kings of the gods— Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, and Vaiśravaṇa—
along with their ministers and retinues [will likewise provide protection].
They rejoiced and praised it, and with reverence they constantly protected and upheld this dhāraṇī. After the Buddha had spoken this sutra,
Śāriputra and all the bhikṣus—
All those in the world— gods, humans, asuras, and others—
hearing what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced;
they received it upon their heads, practiced accordingly, paid homage, and departed.

Dhāraṇī for Knowing Auspiciousness and Misfortune upon Requesting a Dream. Namo to the Triple Gem. Namo to Maṇibhadra, the Great General of Ghosts and Spirits. Mahātata Dhāraṇī. Nirdeśaka-ari-giri. Ari-giri-hūṃ. Tambira-giri. Abaddha-sa. Abaddha-sa. Maṇibhadra-vana. Mahā-kanda-pakanda. The Four Heavenly Kings: Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Virūḍhaka.
Vaiśravaṇa, the King of the Śyāma Gate;
the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; the Yama Heaven;
the Tuṣita Heaven; and the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.
He [is born] among the Yāma devas, the Nirmāṇarati devas,
the Brahmakāyika devas, the Brahmapurohita devas,
the Mahābrahmā devas, and the Ābhāsvara devas.
The Heaven of Subtle Water, the Heaven of Immeasurable Water,
the Heaven of Water’s Response to Merit, the Heaven of Purity by Appointment,
the Heaven of Universal Purity and Clarity, and the Heaven of Guarding the Sublime.
The Subtle Heaven, the Extremely Subtle Heaven,
the Heaven of Merit-Love-Superiority, the Heaven of Near-Attainment,
the Heaven of Universal Observation, and the Heaven of Swift Vision.
The gods of the Heaven Free from Bondage (Anabhraka), the Heaven of Ultimate Purity (Puṇyaprasava),
and the Heaven of Universal Equality (Bṛhatphala)—
these constitute the thirty-three.
Hāṇi hāṇi hāṇi khāṇi khāṇi khāṇi.
Touqie niqie zhique zhique,
recite this mantra over water and give it for people to drink— Ajate.
Parākramasi parāsaṃkramasi parāvirañjani.
Parāparā-muñja-muñjara-te tripurajara-te.
Videhi-hini-ni-ū-kule-mu-khu-dhe-dāna-kṣate.
Dānara-te dāna-saṃtara īpāha. Da-yo-bhī-gi (1) bho-gi (2). Kharu-pāri mahā-pāri śāli mahā-śāli.
Oṃ mahāsāpataye mahāsāpataye apatāsaṅketa.
Dhāraṇī-tathāgata-āgataḥ
Nibbāpeti sabba-dhamme nibbāpeti issa-mada-vippassanā.
Vimalaśubhadharmanirghoṣaruta-nirghoṣāvatī.
Mare cāre hūlu hūlu śobhite mandara mandara.
Sahajīpāṭu jīpāṭu hūṇupāṭu hūṇupāṭu būlupāṭu būlupāṭu.
Cīpācū Cīpācū Ajapācū Dohunā Pācū.
Śamano-pa-cchuh-sudhi-pa-cchu-micchi-hu-na-pa-cchu.
Iho hīna pāñcuni riṭi ṭeṭina pāñcu prajñe ṭeṭina pāñcu.
Migro-nu-hu-ti-na-pa-ju-ut-sru-ti-na-pa-ju.
The Spell for Turning the Bowl of the Sahā Heaven:
Namo maitreyāya, namo maitrāyaśasāya.
Namo maca gagari gathari ganadasi namo siddhārthāya amr̥tavipulavikramiṇe.
Saṃvidha saṃvidhati aṭṭani vaṭṭani vaṭṭa maṇḍa aruhū.
Ṭaṭa saṃgha vime asittadali caṅkuṣṭha paśyanti tārigāthāri.
Gaṇadhipi-nācukṣa.
Buddha-satya dharma-satya saṃgha-satya.
Pratyekabuddha-saṃgha, Arhat-saṃgha, Deva-saṃgha.
The Venerable Saccavaddhano Tāḷiṅgo Tāḷiṅgānaṃ Dīpiko.
Cakṣuṣā svāhā.
Regarding the mirror spell: if one sees a young man, or a person of dignified demeanor, or a foreigner, these are all auspicious signs.
If one sees a practitioner whose appearance is ugly and deformed,
or sees someone weeping and wearing tattered clothes,
these are inauspicious signs.
The *Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Most Victorious Lamp-King of the East*—in the Derge edition of the Tibetan Canon, this is titled the *Sūtra of the Tathāgata Most Victorious Lamp-King of the East*.
Its wording is far more extensive than that of the Song edition, containing many additional passages.
According to the *Kaiyuan lu*,
there were four translations in total, three of which survive and one of which is lost;
this refers to the lost translation from the Eastern Jin dynasty.
It is titled the *Dhāraṇī-pada-sūtra*.
Alternatively, the version lacking the character "pada" (章) is the third translation, which is a missing manuscript.
This present version is the translation by Jñānagupta.
The textual meanings of the Song and Dan editions differ greatly, and their titles also vary slightly;
it is unknown which is correct.
It seems that the Song edition is archaic and质朴 (simple and unadorned).
This does not appear to be a translation by Xuanzang.

Furthermore, since the text repeatedly mentions "dhāraṇī phrases," it is feared that this scripture may be a version of the *Dhāraṇī-phala-sūtra* (the Scripture on the Fruits of Dhāraṇīs) from which the original text was lost.
The Song edition of the Tripitaka lacked the translation by Śikṣānanda, but the *Dongjin shiben tuoluoni jing* (Eastern Jin Lost-Text Dhāraṇī Sūtra) was obtained.
Upon seeing the mention of the "King of the Most Victorious Lamp" (*Dīparāja*) within that sūtra,
it was subsequently identified as the *Dengwang jing* (Lamp King Sūtra) translated by Śikṣānanda.
Otherwise, how could there be such differences in the titles and prefaces of translations by a single person,
and such variations in their extensiveness, brevity, plainness, or literary elegance?
If we now preserve both versions, then the four translations will be complete once again.
